Yes Not now Full Episodes Podcasts Newsletters Live By — Madison Czopek, PolitiFact Madison Czopek, PolitiFact Leave your feedback Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/what-to-know-about-dengue-fever-as-florida-reports-more-than-500-cases-this-year Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What to know about dengue fever as Florida reports more than 500 cases this year Health Updated on Nov 12, 2026 7:57 PM EST — Published on Nov 12, 2026 7:31 PM EST This article originally appeared on PolitiFact. On Nov. 5, low flying helicopters blanketed areas of Florida's Pinellas and Hillsborough counties with a fine mist. It's one of the ways Florida health officials hope to slow the country's largest dengue fever outbreak in more than a decade. READ MORE: Florida's dengue outbreak is largest in continental U.S. in decades Dengue starts with a mosquito bite, so killing the insects is key. The helicopters spray water mixed with Bti, a natural bacteria found in soil that kills black fly and mosquito larvae. Most people become infected when traveling in high dengue risk areas, and Florida had recorded 382 international travel-associated cases as of Oct. 31. But the state has also counted a recent record high number of people infected on Florida's turf: 524. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Florida has had domestic dengue outbreaks before. In 2010, it counted 58 locally acquired cases, after nearly eight decades of reprieve. Since then, the largest outbreak was in 2023, when the state reported 189 dengue cases contracted in Florida. As Florida navigates its largest dengue outbreak in more than 15 years, it might help to understand how this virus spreads and how to recognize symptoms and protect yourself. We sought answers to some pressing dengue fever questions. What is dengue fever? Dengue fever can develop after a person is infected with any of the four dengue viruses. The virus is not transmitted person-to-person, and there is no widely available vaccine to prevent infection. About 3 in 4 people do not get sick, but if symptoms develop, they typically set in about four to 10 days after an infected mosquito's bite. The most common symptoms of mild dengue fever include high fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, rash, pain behind the eyes and muscle, joint and bone pain. About 1 in 20 people infected with a dengue virus develops a more severe form of dengue fever sometimes called dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome. Severe dengue is a life-threatening medical emergency that can cause shock, internal bleeding and death. Warning signs of a severe infection include serious stomach pain or tenderness, vomiting at least three times in 24 hours, bleeding from the gums or nose, rapid breathing, blood in stool or vomit, restlessness, feeling extremely tired and bleeding under the skin that might appear as purplish spots or patches. Those symptoms typically happen 24 to 48 hours after the fever, and they often come on quickly. Anyone experiencing them should seek immediate medical care. What is the treatment for dengue fever? There is no specific cure or treatment. Most people recover in about one week, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said. The CDC recommends people rest, hydrate, and take acetaminophen to reduce fever and pain. Avoid other pain relievers such as aspirin and ibuprofen because they can raise the risk of bleeding. For severe dengue fever, medical professionals might monitor a patient's blood pressure and platelet count and provide blood transfusions or intravenous fluid and electrolyte replacement. Can someone develop immunity to dengue? After being infected with a dengue virus, a person's immune system learns to fight that type of virus, which helps protect them from reinfection with that same virus. But he or she could remain susceptible to the other three dengue viruses. A person might be asymptomatic or have mild symptoms during an initial dengue infection, and then develop more severe symptoms — or, in rare cases, dengue hemorrhagic fever — after being infected with a second type of dengue virus, said Kristi Miley, a University of Florida public health professor. "Dengue is a doozy, mainly because the second infection can be more dangerous than the first," Katelyn Jetelina, an epidemiologist and public health expert, said in social media posts. Florida has documented all four dengue viruses since 2009. The type of dengue virus that's predominantly circulating now "has been noted to cause more severe symptoms than the other three serotypes," Miley said. Why are there so many cases in Florida this year? Florida's climate and environment provides ideal conditions for the Aedes species mosquitoes that spread dengue to thrive. If someone travels to a dengue endemic country and becomes infected even asymptomatically, dengue can enter a community. When a mosquito bites a person infected with the dengue virus, it can introduce the virus to the local mosquito population. An infected female mosquito will remain infected for her life — and she can pass the virus to her eggs, which can result in more than 500 infected offspring, said Miley. WATCH: Florida has a dengue problem. The solution may be more mosquitoes "When you consider the multiplication equation here and add that to the amount of excessive rainfall that the state has been experiencing this late in the year, one can quickly see how an outbreak of this magnitude can happen," she said. All told, the previous 16 years saw only 606 total locally acquired cases. "Studies are ongoing to better understand the factors contributing to the dengue activity being seen in Florida in 2026," said Isabella White, a Florida Department of Health spokesperson. Does the risk extend beyond Florida? Yes. Not every state has the climate to support Aedes mosquito populations, but any state that does could potentially see local transmission of dengue. READ MORE: How climate change will put billions more at risk of mosquito-borne diseases In 2025, CDC data showed locally acquired dengue in Florida, California and Arizona. In August, Virginia health officials reported a locally acquired dengue fever infection. How can people protect themselves and others against dengue? The mosquitoes that carry dengue breed in standing water, so health officials urge people to be vigilant about eliminating it around their homes. "Dump or cover any standing water — especially after each time it rains," Miley said. Florida's Department of Health recommends discarding old tires and drums, emptying and cleaning bird baths or pet water bowls at least once or twice a week and protecting vehicles and boats with tarps so water cannot accumulate. Prevent mosquito bites by using Environmental Protection Agency-registered insect repellants such as deet and picaridin and covering skin with shoes, socks, and long sleeves and pants. The mosquitoes known to carry dengue are often considered "day biters," Miley said. If you suspect you've been infected with the dengue virus, seek medical attention and avoid exposure to mosquitoes for seven days following symptoms — that's how long a person would be able to infect mosquitoes, enabling them to spread the disease, Miley said. excerpt: Florida has reported 624 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026. Here’s what travelers should know about symptoms and avoiding mosquito bites.

What travelers need to know Chris Pugh Wed, November 18, 2026 at 3:24 PM UTC 1 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Florida's dengue outbreak is still growing as winter travel season approaches. The state has reported 624 locally acquired cases in 2026, including 100 newly reported cases during the first week of November, according to the Florida Department of Health. Most infections have been reported around Tampa Bay. Spectrum News reports Hillsborough County has recorded 468 cases, while neighboring Pinellas County has 109. An expert told the outlet that cooler temperatures could slow mosquitoes, but Florida would need a freeze to kill them. The numbers have climbed dramatically since late September, when Florida had 190 locally acquired cases. Earlier in the summer, the outbreak was already drawing attention as locally acquired infections began spreading. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Dengue is a virus that spreads mainly through the bite of an infected mosquito. About 1 in 4 infected people gets sick, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Symptoms can include fever, headache, nausea and muscle or joint pain. Severe dengue is a medical emergency. For people heading to Florida, prevention starts with avoiding mosquito bites. The CDC recommends using insect repellent, wearing loose-fitting long sleeves and pants, and staying in places with air conditioning or window and door screens. People can also help by dumping standing water around homes, where mosquitoes can lay eggs. Federal guidance recommends regularly emptying containers such as buckets, flower pots and pet dishes. Anyone who develops a fever or other dengue symptoms after visiting an affected area should contact a health care provider and mention their travel history. OffOn Stream on As dengue continues to rise in Florida, some are worried about underreporting of cases At least 190 cases of locally acquired dengue have been confirmed in 6 counties. ByMary Kekatos September 30, 2026, 3:00 PM Share Follow ABC News on Google As cases of dengue fever continue to rise in Florida, public health specialists are worried the true number of infections may be greater. For the week ending Sept. 19, at least 190 cases of locally acquired dengue have been confirmed in the state, an increase of 38 cases from the week before, according to data from the Florida Department of Health (DOH). Hillsborough County, which includes Tampa, is reporting the highest number of cases at 170 followed by Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco and Pinellas counties, DOH data shows. Related What to know about dengue fever as Florida reports 1st death and cases rise "There's evidence of local transmission of dengue in several counties in Florida," Natalie Dean, an associate professor of biostatistics and informatics at Emory University's Rollins School of Public Health, told ABC News. "Dengue is not endemic to the United States. That means that it doesn't typically cause local transmission." She added, "There can be occasional outbreaks in the U.S. but this one is notable for its size." Last week, DOH reported the state's first death from dengue fever this year but did not provide any details about the patient including name, age, sex or residence. Close-up of a mosquito biting human skin. Joao Paulo Burini/Getty Images Three counties -- Hillsborough, Pasco and Pinellas -- declared local states of emergency last week. These allow local governments to waive normal procedures, access emergency resources and strengthen efforts to control mosquito populations. Pinellas County crews have been going door to door and spraying areas with high mosquito presence, according to local ABC News affiliate WFTS. "I don't recall a [period] of time when it's been this high in such a sort of concentrated area before," Cameron Wolfe, an infectious diseases specialist and a professor of medicine at Duke University School of Medicine, told ABC News. Wolfe said there may be an underestimate of the true number of cases in Florida. Cases of dengue can be mild, and people may recover on their own or never be tested. Because dengue can resemble a flu-like illness, patients may never suspect the source of their infection. Additionally, he said that reporting of confirmed cases to either local state departments or the CDC can lag. Popular Reads JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions 2 days ago Alaska 2026 live midterm results: Mary Peltola projected winner of Senate seat 1 day ago Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Nov 14 "For every case that we know, there's going to be a bunch that we never find out about," Wolfe said. Related Increased risk of dengue virus infections in the US: CDC Dean added that people can be infected with dengue multiple times over the course of their life, but it's usually the second or later infection that is more severe, leading to further underreporting. "I always think of like the top of an iceberg," Dean said. "We're only capturing some of the some of the cases." The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) told ABC News in a statement on Tuesday that the agency is "closely tracking dengue activity" and the "unprecedented" number of cases in the Tampa area. The CDC also said they've provided $800,000 in emergency funds to help with the response. "Because the types of mosquitoes that spread dengue, Aedes aegypti, are common throughout many areas of the United States, continued local spread of dengue is possible," the CDC statement said. "The best way to prevent dengue is to protect yourself from mosquito bites by using EPA-registered insect repellant, wearing loose fitting clothes, and controlling mosquitoes in and around your home, such as dumping water." Related Dengue fever cases rise to 6,800 in US amid 2 new infections in Los Angeles: CDC Some research has shown that climate change could be expanding the geographic range and severity of dengue fever. Rising global temperature coupled with more rainfall and humidity -- leading to standing water pools that serve as breeding grounds for mosquitoes -- could increase the number of cases. "Global warming and climate change, in fact, leave places like Florida more wet and more capable of housing these mosquito vectors, so I wouldn't be surprised if this becomes a little more of a perpetual thing," Wolfe said. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 19, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Galectin-3 Restricts Dengue Virus Infection Through Envelope Binding and Immune Signaling by November 15, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Galectin-3 Restricts Dengue Virus Infection Through Envelope Binding and Immune Signaling Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram The host protein galectin-3 restricts dengue virus serotype 2 infection by directly binding to the viral envelope glycoprotein, inhibiting viral entry, and enhancing pro-inflammatory NF-κB signaling pathways, according to laboratory and animal findings reported in Virology Journal. Currently, no antiviral therapy is approved for dengue virus, an important pathogen whose pathogenesis remains a major challenge. Galectin-3 is a recognized β-galactoside-binding lectin known to modulate several distinct viral infections, yet its precise mechanistic role in dengue virus infection and disease development had not been previously established. To systematically determine how this lectin influences viral replication, the research team employed a green fluorescent protein-tagged DENV-2 reporter virus across multiple cellular experimental conditions. The investigators evaluated the biological consequences of administering purified recombinant galectin-3, depleting cellular protein levels through targeted knockdown, and increasing cellular protein abundance through experimental overexpression. In addition to assessing replication kinetics, the authors analyzed specific steps in the viral life cycle, focusing on initial viral attachment to host cells and subsequent viral internalization. Initial cellular observations revealed that active DENV-2 infection led to a marked down-regulation of endogenous galectin-3 expression within host cells. When the researchers introduced recombinant galectin-3 into the extracellular environment, the protein caused a dose-dependent reduction in both DENV-2 infectivity and the production of infectious progeny virus. A comparable inhibitory outcome was observed when cells were treated with conditioned medium containing naturally secreted galectin-3, demonstrating that extracellular forms of the lectin exert antiviral activity against the virus. The inhibitory effect of galectin-3 proved to be highly specific and dependent on defined carbohydrate recognition mechanisms. The antiviral restriction exerted by the protein was effectively reversed by the addition of lactose, a known competitive carbohydrate ligand, as well as by the galectin-3-neutralizing monoclonal antibody B2C10. Conversely, neither the control carbohydrate sucrose nor non-specific control immunoglobulin G reversed the observed viral inhibition, confirming that the protective effect relies on specific glycan binding mediated by the lectin. Biochemical and molecular evaluations demonstrated that galectin-3 physically binds the dengue virus envelope glycoprotein, directly hindering both viral attachment and viral internalization into target cells. To clarify the structural basis of this interaction, computational in silico molecular docking was performed against the viral envelope protein. The docking simulations showed that galectin-3 is compatible with engaging both known envelope glycosylation sites, with aggregate computational binding scores favoring interaction at the asparagine-67 (Asn67) glycosylation site. Genetic manipulation of endogenous galectin-3 levels further corroborated its protective role during intracellular infection. Experimental knockdown of endogenous galectin-3 significantly enhanced DENV-2 replication, whereas the overexpression of galectin-3 successfully suppressed viral replication. Concurrently, galectin-3 amplified intracellular NF-κB activation and increased the downstream expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, specifically interleukin-6, interleukin-8, tumor necrosis factor-alpha, and interleukin-1-beta, notably doing so without altering transcripts for type I interferons. To determine whether these in vitro antiviral mechanisms translate into protection within a living organism, the researchers assessed disease outcomes in neonatal galectin-3 knockout mice inoculated intracerebrally with DENV-2. Mice lacking galectin-3 exhibited significantly earlier mortality, carried elevated viral loads within brain tissues, and suffered more severe neuropathology compared to wild-type control animals. These animal results confirmed that endogenous galectin-3 deficiency substantially worsens disease progression and neuropathology in vivo. Together, these findings indicate that galectin-3 restricts dengue virus serotype 2 by binding envelope glycans to block entry and by promoting NF-κB-dependent pro-inflammatory responses. Because galectin-3 deficiency exacerbates infection severity in animal models, the study highlights the lectin as a potential host-directed therapeutic target against dengue virus. However, because these evaluations were conducted in cell culture systems and intracerebrally inoculated neonatal mice, further investigation is required before inferring clinical efficacy or therapeutic utility in human dengue patients. content: Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Boats Grocery Shopping Holidays OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Money Essentials WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services NEWS Dengue fever Add Topic Florida dengue outbreak grows by 100 cases in one week, surges to 624 Cheryl McCloud C. A. Bridges USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Updated Nov. 13, 2026, 3:46 p.m. ET Hear this story Florida is experiencing its largest dengue fever outbreak in decades, with 624 locally acquired cases reported this year. Hillsborough County is the epicenter of the outbreak, with 468 confirmed cases and one death. Recent heavy rainfall may increase the mosquito population and lead to a further rise in cases. The historic surge in dengue fever is getting worse. Florida reported 100 more locally acquired cases in one week, according to the latest update from the Florida Department of Health. The mosquito-borne disease is also called breakbone fever, due to the pain it causes. That brings the statewide total for the year to 624 as of Nov. 7, the largest outbreak in the United States in decades. The previous record for Florida cases in recent memory was 199 in 2023. In 2025, Florida reported 62 cases. The numbers may climb even higher in the weeks ahead after record rainfall left roads flooded, ditches full, and standing water in many Florida yards. ➤ Prevent dengue at home in Florida with this 10-minute mosquito inspection The bulk of the cases continues to be in Hillsborough County on Florida's west coast, which now has 468 confirmed cases. Nearby Pinellas County is now up to 109 cases. Locally acquired cases have been reported in 12 counties. The outbreak prompted Hillsborough County Administrator Bonnie Wise to issue a state of local emergency, which expires Nov. 19 unless the county extends it again as officials "work to control the mosquito population and protect residents from dengue fever." One death has been confirmed in Hillsborough County, identified as 80-year-old Gay Small, who died of “dengue infection” along with septic shock and multi-organ failure, according to a death certificate. Florida's outbreak far exceeds the previous largest outbreak, which was 264 local cases in Hawaii's Big Island between September 2015 and March 2016. President Trump in September issued an order for a "campaign" to reduce the mosquito and tick population in Washington, D.C. That model could then be "applied as targeted, innovative, non-chemical pest control for the whole nation." Dengue isn't the only mosquito-transmitted disease that has been this year in Florida, although those have been in far fewer numbers than dengue: West Nile Virus, Chikungunya and Eastern Equine Encephalitis. Another case each of West Nile and Chikungunya was reported last week. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites, including advice from the Florida Department of Health. 21 counties under mosquito-borne illness advisories, alerts A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Bay Brevard Broward Columbia Holmes Leon Manatee Martin Palm Beach Polk Sarasota Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Citrus Duval Hillsborough Miami-Dade Orange Pasco Pinellas Seminole "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease-capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." Dengue cases continue to climb in Florida According to Florida Department of Health data released Nov. 13, 12 counties have reported 624 locally acquired dengue cases, up from 524 reported Nov. 6. There have also been nine positive samples of locally acquired West Nile virus and two cases of chikungunya. Dengue: 624 cases 468 in Hillsborough County 109 in Pinellas County 16 in Miami-Dade County 14 in Orange County 6 in Pasco County 3 in Citrus County 2 in Manatee County 2 in Seminole County 1 in Brevard County 1 in Broward County 1 in Palm Beach County 1 in Polk County West Nile: nine cases 2 in Alachua County 2 in Duval County (including one asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Columbia County 1 in Holmes County 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Sarasota County 1 in Walton County Chikungunya: 2 cases 2 in Miami-Dade County Eastern Equine Encephalitis: 1 case 1 in Leon County Florida health officials have also reported 422 cases of dengue in victims who traveled from a dengue-endemic area within two weeks of onset. Counties reporting international-travel-associated cases were: Alachua, Bay, Brevard (4), Broward (20), Collier (5), Duval (3), Hendry, Hernando, Hillsborough (26), Lake, Lee (19), Manatee (3), Marion (2), Miami-Dade (271), Monroe (3), Orange (8), Osceola (3), Palm Beach (20), Pasco (3), Pinellas (4), Polk (4), Sarasota (2), Seminole (4), St. Johns (4), St. Lucie (8), and Walton. Six cases were reported in non-Florida residents. What is Hillsborough County doing to try to control mosquitoes? "Mosquito management crews are increasing treatments by air and ground because the county’s mosquito surveillance in many neighborhoods is showing dengue virus activity in the mosquito population. "Residents are encouraged to look for and eliminate standing water on their property after recent heavy rains." Residents can sign up to be notified where aerial treatment will occur in neighborhoods. You can also go to the county's website to see when and where mosquito "operations" are scheduled to take place. Florida residents should take precautions to avoid mosquito-borne illnesses "Residents throughout the state should continue to take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying bug spray, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible — especially during sunrise and sunset when mosquitos are most active," said Isabella White, FDOH press secretary via email Sept. 23. White said FDOH "continues to coordinate with local mosquito control partners to support surveillance and targeted response efforts in affected areas. These efforts help reduce mosquito populations, limit the risk of disease transmission, and protect residents across Florida." What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Why is dengue called 'breakbone fever?' Dengue is sometimes called “breakbone fever” because, in addition to fever, "it can cause severe aches and pains, especially in the legs, joints, and back," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue does not actually cause bones to break, according to YaleMedicine. Is dengue contagious? Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight, or premature birth. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. The whole province has recorded more than 12,200 cases, including 2 deaths. Dengue fever diễn biến phức tạp, treatment pressure in Dak Lak increases. During the day, the locality did not record any more deaths. content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Medical Dengue fever threatens even young, healthy people; prevention measures need to be strengthened. A 24-year-old man with dengue fever had to be placed on a cardiopulmonary bypass machine due to complications including fulminant myocarditis and multiple organ failure, demonstrating the severity of the disease even in young people. Check Symptoms Báo Đầu tư•17/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 With the country recording over 170,000 cases and 21 deaths, experts recommend combining mosquito control, early detection of worsening symptoms, and proactive disease prevention measures. Dengue fever continues to be a complex issue in many localities, with an increasing number of cases and unpredictable complications. Worryingly, the disease can progress rapidly, causing shock, severe bleeding, damage to the heart, liver, and kidneys, and even threatening the lives of previously healthy individuals. The case of a 24-year-old man in Ho Chi Minh City who was recently saved by doctors at Gia Dinh People's Hospital after developing complications from fulminant myocarditis serves as a warning about the dangers of this infectious disease, which is often underestimated in its early stages. Mr. NKL (24 years old, residing in Vung Tau area, Ho Chi Minh City) suddenly developed symptoms of high fever, chest pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. On November 2nd, the patient was taken to Vung Tau General Hospital for emergency treatment in a state of hypotension. Find Treatments In Vietnam, the dengue fever vaccine is licensed for use in people aged 4 years and older, with a two-dose schedule administered three months apart. Recognizing that the patient was exhibiting severe cardiogenic shock and had a high risk of death, the doctors quickly consulted and transferred him to Gia Dinh People's Hospital for further specialized treatment. Here, the patient's condition deteriorated significantly. Blood pressure continued to drop sharply, forcing the resuscitation team to use high doses of vasopressors and inotropic agents to maintain circulation. Echocardiogram results revealed severely impaired myocardial contractility, while laboratory tests showed extensive myocardial damage, along with impaired liver and kidney function. Find Treatments Notably, test results confirmed the patient was positive for the Dengue virus. Doctors diagnosed the patient with cardiogenic shock due to fulminant myocarditis associated with dengue fever, accompanied by multiple organ failure. Faced with imminent death, the resuscitation team decided to deploy VA-ECMO, a cardiopulmonary bypass system, to support circulation and allow the damaged heart muscle and organs time to recover. After a week of intensive treatment, the patient's heart function gradually improved. The patient was weaned off vasopressors, ECMO was discontinued, mobility was restored, and the patient was discharged. According to the patient's treating physician, fulminant myocarditis associated with dengue fever is a particularly dangerous complication with a high risk of death, even in young people without underlying medical conditions. Check Symptoms According to doctors, ECMO does not directly treat the cause of the disease but plays a temporary role in supporting vital functions, giving damaged organs more time to recover. The effectiveness of treatment depends on the timing of intervention, the extent of damage, and the ability to coordinate intensive resuscitation measures. This case demonstrates that dengue fever is not simply a disease causing fever, headache, body aches, or low platelet count. In severe cases, the dengue virus can be associated with multi-organ damage, circulatory disorders, and can push patients into critical condition in a short period of time. You may also like One of the worrying risks is that the disease can worsen during the fever phase, usually about 3-7 days after onset. Patients and their families may mistakenly believe their health is improving, while the body may experience plasma leakage, blood concentration, shock, or other serious complications. Find Treatments Symptoms such as severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, extreme fatigue, restlessness, lethargy, cold extremities, decreased urination, or shortness of breath should be given special attention. If chest pain, shortness of breath, or signs of hypotension occur, the patient needs immediate emergency care to assess the risk of heart damage and circulatory disorders. Not only the elderly, children, or those with underlying health conditions, but even young, healthy people can experience severe complications from dengue fever. Therefore, timely examination and close monitoring of the disease's progression are crucial in reducing the risk of death. Data released by the Department of Disease Prevention, Ministry of Health, at the Dengue Fever Conference 2026 shows that in the first 10 months of the year, the whole country recorded 170,684 cases and 21 deaths. The number of cases increased by about 26% compared to the same period last year, reflecting the increasing pressure on disease prevention and control efforts. Notably, dengue fever is circulating year-round in many localities, with all four types of the Dengue virus coexisting. Weather fluctuations, urbanization, and favorable conditions for mosquito breeding make the disease increasingly difficult to predict. The risk of reinfection also poses a challenge to disease prevention efforts. People who have previously had dengue fever can still be infected with a different type of dengue virus, while some subsequent infections carry a higher risk of more severe symptoms. Check Symptoms Given the complex situation with dengue fever, health experts emphasize the need to shift strongly towards proactive disease prevention, combining control of disease-transmitting mosquitoes, raising community awareness, early detection of cases, and implementing appropriate vaccination programs. In this context, eliminating the breeding grounds of Aedes mosquitoes remains the fundamental solution. People need to regularly clean their homes, cover water containers tightly, remove items that collect water, change the water in flower vases, and cooperate with health authorities in activities to eliminate mosquito larvae and treat outbreaks. In addition, it is necessary to prevent mosquito bites by wearing long clothing, using appropriate mosquito repellent products, installing mosquito nets on windows, and implementing personal protective measures. Mosquitoes that transmit dengue fever are usually most active during the day, so mosquito prevention needs to be maintained regularly. Along with vector control measures, the availability of dengue fever vaccines has added another preventive tool, contributing to a reduction in the risk of illness and hospitalization for those recommended for vaccination. In Vietnam, the dengue fever vaccine is licensed for use in people aged 4 years and older, with a two-dose schedule administered three months apart. This is a live attenuated vaccine, developed to generate an immune response against four types of dengue virus. Ms. Do Cao Van Anh, a senior advisory board expert at Long Chau Pharmacy and Vaccination System, stated that individuals who have or have not had dengue fever can be assessed for vaccination; prior testing for dengue infection is not mandatory. You may also like Notably, vaccination should be administered according to professional guidelines, especially for individuals with underlying medical conditions or special health circumstances. The vaccine is contraindicated for pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers, individuals with significant immunosuppression, and those with a history of severe hypersensitivity reactions to vaccine components or previous doses. Individuals with acute illnesses and high fevers should postpone vaccination until their health stabilizes. For those who have recently recovered from dengue fever, the timing of vaccination should be advised by a doctor; some guidelines recommend waiting about six months after recovery. Women planning to become pregnant should complete vaccination at least one month before their expected pregnancy. In addition, people currently suffering from dengue fever should prioritize treatment and monitoring for warning signs, and should not receive vaccinations during the acute phase of the disease. Vaccination after recovery must be evaluated through a screening examination to ensure safety. However, experts agree that vaccines cannot replace measures to prevent mosquito bites and eliminate mosquito breeding grounds. Dengue fever is not transmitted directly through shaking hands, talking, or hugging, but mainly through Aedes mosquitoes carrying the virus. Therefore, controlling the disease vector remains crucial in epidemic prevention. The health sector recommends that each family spend at least 10 minutes each week checking for and removing stagnant water sources and mosquito larvae inside and outside the house. Easily overlooked places such as flower vases, water cups on altars, plant pot saucers, water containers, or discarded bottles and cans can all become breeding grounds for mosquitoes. In fact, even a very small amount of water remaining in a can lid or forgotten item can create ideal conditions for mosquitoes to lay eggs. Therefore, covering water containers, collecting waste, turning unused items upside down, and proactively preventing mosquito bites should become regular habits. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 19, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Timor-Leste Dengue Modeling Reveals Widespread Infection Risk and Sharp Coastal Hotspots by November 16, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Timor-Leste Dengue Modeling Reveals Widespread Infection Risk and Sharp Coastal Hotspots Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A nationwide, population-representative serosurvey conducted across Timor-Leste has revealed that dengue virus transmission is extensive across the country, showing pronounced spatial variation and severe hotspots of infection risk along northern and eastern coastal zones. By combining empirical age-stratified antibody detection with Bayesian sero-catalytic and geostatistical modeling, investigators established that the annual per-capita risk of dengue virus infection for a susceptible individual exceeded five percent across most geographic areas. The findings provide the first high-resolution, nationwide transmission map for the country, demonstrating substantial disease circulation in rural communities that have historically been underrepresented in case-based clinical surveillance records. Dengue virus infection represents a major global health burden across tropical and subtropical environments, producing severe clinical manifestations including dengue haemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome alongside extensive asymptomatic or self-limiting illness. In Timor-Leste, routine public health surveillance has historically depended upon case notifications from healthcare facilities, which systematically under-report true infection counts due to uneven healthcare-seeking behaviors, diagnostic barriers, and regional resource disparities. Because previous serological investigations in the country were limited to a single unrepresentative pilot study carried out between late 2018 and early 2019, the comprehensive geographic scope and underlying drivers of dengue transmission across rural and urban districts had remained uncharacterized until now. To evaluate transmission dynamics across diverse administrative landscapes, the investigative team deployed a three-stage cluster sampling design informed by World Health Organization cluster survey guidelines. Fieldwork executed between October 2021 and February 2023 randomly sampled households derived from the 2015 national housing census across 113 enumeration areas proportionate to municipal population sizes. Field teams successfully visited 102 enumeration areas across all thirteen administrative municipalities of Timor-Leste, achieving an enumeration area participation rate of 90.3 percent. Logistical barriers, including severe weather, impassable roads, time constraints, and staff illness, prevented sampling in eleven originally targeted enumeration areas. Discover more Check Symptoms Infectious disease Study Biology Infectious Disease infections The serological dataset ultimately incorporated 4780 individuals residing within 1755 households across the 102 sampled enumeration areas, representing a household participation rate of 67.2 percent and an individual participation rate of 56.7 percent among enumerated occupants. The median participant age was 28 years with an inter-quartile range spanning 13 to 46 years, and female participants accounted for 59.2 percent of the sampled cohort. Demonstrating the representative demographic coverage of the survey across dispersed settlements, 73.0 percent of the participants resided in households classified as rural during the national census. Venous blood samples were collected via phlebotomy from consenting household occupants aged above one year, with target blood volumes stratified between children and adult cohorts. Collected serum specimens were transported under controlled refrigeration to the Laboratorio Nacional de Saude in Dili and evaluated using the commercial Panbio Indirect dengue IgG enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. This diagnostic assay measures human IgG antibodies directed against any dengue virus serotype, functioning as a marker of past lifetime infection rather than acute illness. Testing identified dengue IgG antibodies in 3931 individuals, yielding an overall raw seropositivity rate of 83.1 percent among participants. A small fraction of samples, comprising 57 individuals or 1.2 percent of the total dataset, fell into the manufacturer-defined equivocal index value range between 0.9 and 1.1 and were conservatively categorized as seronegative in the primary analysis. Discover more health Get Health Tips Get Risk Software To translate binary cross-sectional antibody measures into an interpretable metric of exposure, researchers constructed a hierarchical Bayesian catalytic model. Operating under the epidemiological assumption of endemic equilibrium, the catalytic framework leverages participant age as an indicator of cumulative time at risk, parsing age-dependent seroprevalence curves into force-of-infection estimates. The statistical architecture represented force of infection on the logit scale, nesting individual probabilities within households and households within enumeration areas to account explicitly for intra-household clustering effects. In addition, the model directly estimated imperfect diagnostic accuracy, identifying an assay sensitivity of 99 percent and an assay specificity of 98 percent from the empirical data. The sero-catalytic analysis demonstrated intense spatial heterogeneity in transmission intensity across the surveyed enumeration areas, with median force-of-infection values varying by more than fifty-fold across different locales. Estimated median annual force of infection ranged from a low of 0.010, with a 95 percent credible interval spanning 0.005 to 0.018, in enumeration area 10104032 located in Fatubossa within Aileu municipality, to a high of 0.519, with a credible interval spanning 0.295 to 0.816, in enumeration area 40403012 in Goulolo within Bobonaro municipality. Enumeration areas situated in Bobonaro, Dili, Atauro Island, and Baucau exhibited the highest localized transmission metrics, whereas inland mountainous jurisdictions such as Aileu, Ainaro, and Ermera consistently demonstrated the lowest transmission values. Discover more Buy Maps Learn Tagalog Explore History Find Treatments Health To investigate the environmental and climatic determinants governing these spatial patterns, the researchers matched the enumeration area force-of-infection estimates with decadal gridded satellite observations spanning 2011 to 2022. Using stochastic partial differential equations within integrated nested Laplace approximations, the team fitted spatial regression models examining multi-year averages of temperature extremes, vapor pressure, accumulated rainfall, elevation, mid-infrared reflectance, and enhanced vegetation index. Spatial regression analysis established that relative humidity exhibited a significant negative association with dengue virus force of infection. Across the joint posterior distributions, the median regression coefficient for relative humidity at minimum temperature was negative 0.96 with a 95 percent credible interval between negative 1.47 and negative 0.39, while relative humidity at maximum temperature yielded a median coefficient of negative 0.65 with a credible interval between negative 1.20 and negative 0.13. By contrast, enhanced vegetation index showed no statistically significant association with transmission intensity. The inverse relationship with relative humidity corresponds with local geographic gradients, where humidity peaks in elevated, cool mountain terrain but drops along warmer, highly populated coastal plains where mosquito proliferation and human biting rates are concentrated. Extrapolating model dynamics across all 2350 enumeration areas in Timor-Leste generated comprehensive nationwide predictions of transmission risk and expected pediatric immunity. The predictive models pinpointed the highest exposure rates along the northern and eastern coastlines, identifying prominent transmission hubs in urban centers such as Dili, Baucau, and Manatuto, as well as on Atauro Island. When aggregated to municipal boundaries, Atauro Island and Dili municipality displayed median predicted annual force-of-infection rates of 0.27 and 0.22, translating to anticipated median seroprevalence proportions at nine years of age of 91 percent and 86 percent, respectively. Municipalities including Lautem, Liquica, and Baucau similarly sustained force-of-infection values exceeding 0.15, corresponding to an expected nine-year-old seroprevalence above 74 percent. Conversely, high-altitude interior regions experienced substantially attenuated transmission intensities, with Aileu, Ainaro, and Ermera municipalities presenting median force-of-infection estimates below 0.05 and expected seroprevalence at age nine falling below 36 percent. The stark contrast between coastal lowlands and mountainous interiors underscores the role of local geography in shaping arboviral exposure. Furthermore, the identification of high transmission rates across rural sectors with negligible historic case reporting highlights the degree to which facility-based surveillance fails to detect widespread mild or subclinical infections, particularly where geographic isolation and limited clinical infrastructure restrict access to formal medical evaluations. The authors noted specific methodological limitations inherent to the survey design and historical datasets. Relying on sampling frames derived from the 2015 national housing census meant structural shifts in dwelling occupancy over the intervening six years could have introduced minor sampling discrepancies, though post-independence stabilization has reduced internal displacement. Additionally, assigning infection exposure to a participant’s current residence cannot fully capture infections acquired during travel between enumeration areas, and the time-constant modeling formulation does not estimate seasonal or interannual outbreak surges. Gridded environmental variables derived at spatial scales between one and five kilometers also necessitated spatial averaging across smaller enumeration areas. Despite these analytical caveats, the nationwide serosurvey establishes an essential baseline for contemporary public health decision-making in Timor-Leste. The reconstructed seroprevalence metrics at nine years of age provide specific empirical parameters mandated by World Health Organization frameworks to evaluate the programmatic introduction of dengue vaccines, such as TAK-003. Furthermore, the high-resolution mapping of transmission hotspots offers operational guidance for mosquito abatement initiatives and the targeted deployment of Wolbachia-infected mosquito release programs, ensuring vector control resources are directed toward communities bearing the highest cumulative infection burden. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 19, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Dengue Dimer Epitope Antibodies Link to Protection From Severe Secondary Infection by November 14, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Dengue Dimer Epitope Antibodies Link to Protection From Severe Secondary Infection Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Antibodies targeting quaternary epitopes across the envelope protein dimer interface correlate with protection against severe dengue disease in patients undergoing secondary dengue virus infection, according to findings from clinical cohorts in Cambodia and Colombia. In contrast, antibodies directed against the conserved envelope fusion loop were found at significantly elevated proportions in hospitalized patients compared with individuals who experienced subclinical infections. Functionally, purified human antibody fractions directed against the soluble envelope dimer demonstrated potent virus neutralization and cross-neutralization against distinct serotypes while exhibiting limited enhancement of cellular infection. Conversely, antibodies recognizing the fusion loop mediated weak neutralization and pronounced antibody-dependent enhancement in Fc-receptor-bearing cells in vitro, clarifying how distinct antibody subsets directed toward the same viral surface protein can drive divergent clinical trajectories during natural post-primary dengue virus exposure. The dengue virus envelope glycoprotein is the primary target of human humoral immunity and is organized on mature virions into ninety homodimers arranged in an antiparallel head-to-tail lattice. Each monomeric envelope subunit comprises three structural regions designated domain one, domain two, and domain three, which together mediate cell attachment and acid-triggered membrane fusion. Within domain two, a hydrophobic fusion loop sequence remains highly conserved across all four dengue virus serotypes as well as related flaviviruses, yet its accessibility on mature virions is structurally constrained beneath neighboring envelope subunits. At the contact boundary formed between two paired envelope monomers, virus assembly generates a quaternary conformational target known as the envelope dimer epitope. While monoclonal antibodies against these respective sites have previously shown differing neutralization profiles in cell culture and animal models, their relative prevalence and direct association with human clinical severity across natural post-primary infections have historically remained unresolved. To investigate these epitope-specific antibody dynamics during active illness, investigators analyzed longitudinal plasma samples collected from children recruited into the prospective DENTHOM project across Kampong Thom and Siem Reap provinces in Cambodia. Patients admitted to Kampong Thom Provincial Hospital, Baray District Hospital, Stuong District Hospital, and Jayavarman VII Hospital with acute febrile illness were confirmed for secondary dengue virus serotype two infection using quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction alongside hemagglutination inhibition assays. Hospitalized cases were clinically classified according to World Health Organization criteria into classic dengue fever or severe manifestations comprising dengue hemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome. Concurrently, household contact investigations surrounding laboratory-confirmed index cases identified infected individuals who developed subclinical infections, defined by absent or mild fever not exceeding thirty-eight degrees Celsius for at most two consecutive days and no more than one accompanying symptom such as rash, nausea, or aches. Using a multiplex microsphere-based immunoassay, the team tracked antibody binding against recombinant soluble envelope monomers, envelope domain three, and engineered soluble envelope dimers produced in Drosophila S2 cells harboring cysteine substitutions at residues leucine 107 and alanine 313. These engineered disulfide bonds preserve the envelope dimer conformation and prevent exposure of the internal fusion loop. By comparing untreated plasma binding against binding following competitive blockade with the pan-flavivirus monoclonal antibody clone 4G2, researchers quantified the exact proportions of fusion loop-targeting antibodies and dimer-specific quaternary antibodies throughout the acute, critical, early recovery, and late recovery phases. Across all post-primary infection phases, antibody concentrations recognizing domain three remained substantially lower than antibodies binding soluble envelope monomers and total soluble envelope dimers, demonstrating that domain three contributes only a modest share of the circulating polyclonal response in naturally infected pediatric patients. Epitope-specific antibody levels exhibited substantial inter-individual variability during early symptomatic presentation but increased markedly over time, reaching peak titers across the critical and early convalescent stages between four and fourteen days following symptom onset. During the acute phase spanning the initial three days of illness, detectable levels of dimer-specific antibodies were present in similar frequencies between subclinical and hospitalized individuals, and no differences in antibody proportions emerged when hospitalized patients were stratified by clinical severity. However, substantial divergence developed during the critical phase four to six days post-onset, which coincides with active viremia and the potential development of plasma leakage. Hospitalized patients showed significantly higher proportions of fusion loop-directed antibodies than individuals with subclinical infection, indicating that elevated proportions of poorly neutralizing, cross-reactive fusion loop antibodies in the critical window correlate with greater disease susceptibility. Among hospitalized children evaluated during the critical phase, the proportion of envelope dimer-specific antibodies proved significantly lower in severe dengue cases with hemorrhagic fever or shock syndrome than in children presenting with uncomplicated dengue fever. Median dimer-specific antibody proportions measured zero point twelve in severe cases compared with zero point thirty-seven in dengue fever, demonstrating a statistically significant protective association. To evaluate whether this immunological pattern extended across different viral serotypes and distinct host populations, the researchers examined an independent adult validation cohort from Cali and Bucaramanga, Colombia, comprising patients undergoing secondary dengue virus serotype one infection diagnosed by multiplex reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction and high-avidity immunoglobulin G enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. In the Colombian cohort, hospitalized patients with classic dengue similarly exhibited higher median proportions of serotype one dimer-specific antibodies than those who progressed to severe disease, reinforcing the protective association across geographically distinct populations. To establish the mechanistic properties of these antibody populations directly from patient circulation rather than synthetic monoclonal surrogates, the investigators isolated total polyclonal immunoglobulin G from twelve Cambodian pediatric patients sampled during the critical phase. Utilizing sequential resin affinity chromatography coupled with site-specifically biotinylated recombinant envelope antigens, the authors successfully fractionated domain three antibodies, envelope dimer-specific antibodies, and fusion loop-reactive antibodies. Subsequent immunoassay binding validation confirmed that the dimer-specific fraction selectively recognized envelope dimers without cross-reacting with domain three, whereas the isolated fusion loop fraction bound preferentially to soluble monomeric envelope proteins displaying the exposed fusion motif while showing minimal reactivity against stabilized dimers or isolated domain three proteins. Functional evaluation using flow cytometry neutralization assays in Vero CCL-81 cells revealed that the purified envelope dimer-specific fraction possessed markedly superior neutralizing potency against dengue virus serotype two compared with fusion loop-binding antibodies. Dimer-specific antibodies achieved fifty percent viral neutralization at a median concentration of fifty-five point six nanograms per milliliter, whereas fusion loop antibodies required a significantly higher median concentration of one hundred forty-seven point four nanograms per milliliter to reach equivalent inhibition. Conversely, selective depletion of domain three, monomeric soluble envelope, and envelope dimer antibodies completely eliminated neutralization capacity while retaining residual infection enhancement, an effect likely maintained by non-neutralizing antibodies targeting structural pre-membrane proteins that remain on partially mature virus particles. Infection enhancement assays performed using engineered U937 monocyte cell lines expressing Fc-gamma receptors one, two-a, two-b, and three demonstrated that fusion loop antibodies generated substantially higher rates of antibody-dependent enhancement than dimer-specific or domain three fractions. At a test concentration of three hundred nanograms per milliliter, fusion loop-targeting antibodies induced productive infection in thirty point five percent of cells, compared with sixteen point three percent for domain three antibodies and fourteen point four percent for envelope dimer-specific antibodies. Even when normalized to their respective fifty percent inhibitory concentrations, fusion loop antibodies provoked over thirty percent cellular infection enhancement, roughly double the enhancement frequency observed for dimer-specific antibodies, confirming that fusion loop-directed antibodies display intrinsically heightened enhancing capacity under equivalent neutralization thresholds. Cross-neutralization experiments further underscored the distinct functional utility of envelope dimer antibodies when challenged with heterologous viral serotypes. When tested against dengue virus serotype one, dimer-specific antibodies isolated from serotype two-infected donors demonstrated potent cross-protective efficacy, achieving fifty percent inhibition at a median concentration of two point eighty-three nanograms per milliliter. In contrast, domain three fractions required a median of eighty-two point twenty-nine nanograms per milliliter, and fusion loop antibodies required four hundred eighty-one point one nanograms per milliliter to achieve fifty percent neutralization. These data confirm that while domain three-specific antibodies remain predominantly homotypic, human antibodies directed against the quaternary dimer interface mediate potent cross-serotype neutralization across genetically divergent dengue lineages. The study notes several methodological constraints and biological limitations that contextualize these immunological findings. Competitive blockade relied on mouse monoclonal antibody 4G2 to define fusion loop specificity, which might fail to detect human antibodies binding adjacent overlapping contacts or underestimate high-affinity human antibodies that outcompete the blocking clone. Furthermore, in vitro neutralization assays utilized virus stocks propagated in C6/36 mosquito cell lines, which harbor variable mixtures of immature and partially mature virions whose exposed structural surfaces can alter epitope accessibility compared with fully mature virus structures encountered in vivo. Clinically, determination of past dengue exposure relied on hemagglutination inhibition and antibody avidity assays, which cannot distinguish whether an individual has experienced exactly one prior infection or multiple tertiary and quaternary exposures that naturally skew antibody repertoires toward broader neutralizing profiles. Despite these considerations, the findings establish that the epitope specificity of the polyclonal envelope antibody repertoire represents a pivotal correlate of human dengue infection outcome. The data indicate that high relative proportions of fusion loop antibodies during the critical phase associate with symptomatic progression and hospitalization through Fc-mediated enhancement, whereas abundant quaternary dimer-targeting antibodies reduce disease severity and confer broad cross-neutralizing coverage. These observations offer direct immunological targets for vaccine design, indicating that next-generation immunization platforms should aim to present conformationally intact envelope dimers that elicit protective quaternary responses while minimizing the presentation of accessible, enhancement-prone fusion loop structures. content: Featured Columns about 2 months ago The Clean Bite: Making Dental Infection Control Part of Every Day about 2 months ago Pathogen Pulse: The Alarming Rise of Dengue in Florida 3 months ago Bug of the Month: You Never See Me Coming Shorts Podcasts Sterile Processing Burnout and Cognitive Overload: How Interruptions, IFUs, and Human Factors Affect Patient Safety Sterile processing professionals face constant interruptions, cognitive overload, increasingly complex devices, and hundreds of IFUs. Randalyn Harreld, CRCST, FHSPA, explains why health care organizations must address the human factors behind SPD performance rather than expecting frontline professionals to simply absorb ever-increasing complexity. From “Gotcha” to Coaching: Using RTLS to Improve Hand Hygiene In this podcast with ICT, Danielle Updegraff, MBA, BSN, RN, discusses real-time location systems, which can give infection prevention teams greater visibility into hand hygiene, workflow, and infectious disease exposures, but sustainable improvement still depends on staff engagement, leadership, education, and culture. AIDS 2026: Malawi Program Achieves 10-fold Reduction in HIV Positivity Among Exposed Infants In this complete interview, ICT speaks with Endale Tilahun, MD, MPH, about a Malawi community program that reduced missed HIV testing and achieved 0.2% positivity among exposed infants through household follow-up, individualized case management, and coordinated health and social support. Experts Call for Standardized Cleaning of Reusable Lead Aprons Environmental testing found bacterial contamination on many lead garments and described what lead garment cleaning technicians routinely encounter during servicing. AIDS 2026 Research Shows Individualized HIV Treatment Is Shaping the Future New research presented at AIDS 2026 indicates that 2-drug HIV regimens and long-acting injectable therapies are effective treatment options that also enhance personalized care. Investigators highlight that shared decision-making, adherence, quality of life, and minimizing long-term medication exposure are becoming more vital alongside maintaining viral suppression. Contagious Conversations: Global Infection Prevention Leaders Say the Future of IPC Depends on Diverse Career Pathways International infection prevention leaders discuss how Ireland and Saudi Arabia educate, recruit, and prepare IPC professionals while advocating for broader, multidisciplinary career pathways worldwide. Hantavirus: A Podcast With an Infectious Disease Doctor A hantavirus outbreak linked to a South American cruise ship is drawing global attention, but experts say fears of a COVID-19-style pandemic are largely unsupported. Infectious disease physician Matthew Pullen, MD, discusses Andes virus transmission, misinformation, cruise ship risks, and what health care professionals should really be watching for. Contagious Conversations: SoCal SPA Chapter Conference Highlights How Voice, Mentorship, and Everyday Practice Drive Leadership and Patient Safety The cohosts of Contagious Conversation speak with Tori Whitacre Martonicz, lead editor of Infection Control Today, about her presentation at the SoCal SPA Spring Conference, and how the conference speakers emphasized leadership beyond titles, urging SPD professionals to share knowledge, speak up, and turn everyday insights into safer patient care practices. The Invisible Heroes: Why Dental Assistant Recognition Week Matters (Podcast) Dental assistants manage sterilization, infection control, and patient education—yet most states require zero formal training. They earn the lowest wages in dental offices. Meet Sherrie Busby's 42-year mission to secure standardized credentialing and fair recognition. (Audio podcast) ICTalk Podcast: 2025 APIC President Carol McLay, DrPH, Reflects on Advocacy, Global Collaboration, and the Future of Infection Prevention As her 2025 APIC presidency concludes, Carol McLay, DrPH, MPH, RN, CIC, FAPIC, FSHEA, discusses public health funding cuts, science advocacy, global partnerships, workforce development, and why infection preventionists must speak up. In this exclusive ICT interview, she shares lessons from a tumultuous year and her vision for strengthening the infection prevention profession worldwide. All News What happens to a towel between uses? Natasha Terborg traces the laundry process from collection to storage and explains which practices from health care guidance can inform everyday laundry in shared facilities. An infection preventionist examines the DRC’s Ebola response through contact tracing and community engagement, explaining why daily follow-up, timely investigations, and trust reveal challenges that cumulative case counts alone cannot capture. Four vaccine experts discuss how sustained financing, local research leadership, and community trust can strengthen vaccine development in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), drawing on practical insights from India and Bangladesh. GeoVax CEO David Dodd discusses how vaccine storage requirements, supplier diversification, and regional manufacturing shape outbreak preparedness, with considerations for infection preventionists and health systems preparing to receive and administer doses. Part 4 of 4: Why better planning for surgical growth, operational performance, and patient safety requires sterile processing expertise early in the decision-making process. An emerging cause of sexually transmitted ringworm, TMVII can resemble other skin conditions and require prolonged treatment. Learn what clinicians and infection preventionists should know about recognition, specialized testing, and patient counseling. The Next Generation of SPD Leadership: Human Plus Machine 3 of 4: How technology, artificial intelligence, automation, and data are reshaping sterile processing leadership The Next Generation of SPD Leadership: Building the Workforce of the Future Part 2 of 4: Recruitment may bring people into sterile processing. Development is what determines whether they stay. At IDWeek 2026, Rachel Sidebottom discusses research exploring phage-antibiotic combinations, the potential for predictive modeling, and an investigation identifying an ST5 strain of nontoxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae circulating in Albuquerque. Finding infections earlier is only part of the work. At IDWeek 2026, David Weber, MD, MPH, explored how broader surveillance and emerging technologies could help infection preventionists spend more time supporting safer care. Two experts give an update ahead of the first season with a new mRNA vaccine against flu. The Next Generation of SPD Leadership: People First, Standards Always Part 1 of 4: How emerging sterile processing leaders are redefining leadership through trust, accountability, psychological safety, and professional development. This week in infection prevention: Kenya’s Bundibugyo virus response shows why execution, not just planning, determines outcomes, and France reported the first known human Shamonda virus infection. Our roundup also covers brucellosis, blood donor screening, and long-acting HIV antibody findings from IDWeek 2026. At IDWeek 2026, Jimmy Chang, PhD, discussed investigational HIV antibodies TMB-365 and TMB-380, explaining their complementary mechanisms, early study findings, and ongoing evaluation as a long-acting maintenance regimen. At IDWeek 2026, Samuel Ntow, MBChB, MPH, discussed research findings of reactive infection screening markers in 18.3% of replacement donor records from rural Ghana, highlighting opportunities for further evaluation and linkage to care. France’s first reported human Shamonda virus infection raises questions about transmission and vulnerable patients. Explore what investigators know, what remains uncertain, and why infection preventionists should follow this emerging story. John Rex, MD, CMO of F2G, discusses investigational olorofim’s phase 3 findings, why new antifungals are difficult to develop, and how an oral option could help patients with limited treatment choices. An analysis of 147 million US hospital admissions identified 875 adults with brucellosis diagnoses, highlighting demographic and regional differences while emphasizing exposure histories and uncertainty about underdiagnosis. Kenya’s secondary Ebola cases raise urgent questions about hospital readiness. Explore what the response reveals about contact tracing, health care worker protection, and the implementation of infection prevention plans. An ICU study found that alcohol-based hand rub applied after patient care reduced glove bioburden, while staff raised feasibility concerns. Researchers stress that the practice does not replace glove changes or hand hygiene. A study of 4,851 nursing home residents linked shared rooms to higher odds of matching MDRO carriage, while universal decolonization was associated with lower concordant carriage across MRSA, ESBL, and VRE. A retrospective hospital study found no significant differences in mortality or readmissions between infectious disease e-consults and in-person consultations, despite more diagnoses of bacteremia among e-consult patients. Researchers recommend further evaluation across settings. Presented at IDWeek 2026, a living review of 64 studies found the strongest evidence for dengue prevention from mosquito modification, while highlighting substantial uncertainty and research gaps in other approaches to Aedes vector control. A 2026 IDWeek poster details how respiratory cultures and whole genome sequencing clarified a NICU MRSA outbreak, with targeted prevention measures followed by at least 6 months without additional bacteremias or related respiratory clusters. Researchers recovered a carbapenemase-producing organism from the shaft of a hospital drain auger, prompting calls for standardized reprocessing protocols and further investigation into maintenance equipment as a potential source of environmental dissemination. A poster presented at IDWeek was a systematic review of 35 studies that found rare transmission of viral hemorrhagic fever to health care personnel in high-income countries and highlighted the need for standardized exposure definitions to guide response. Kimberley Brown, PharmD, Head of U.S. Medical Affairs at ViiV Healthcare discusses the evolution of HIV care and how innovative long-acting injectables are expanding options across HIV treatment and prevention. Clean Hospitals President Alexandra Peters, PhD, explains how training, meaningful support, and stronger collaboration with infection prevention teams can empower environmental services staff and strengthen patient safety. A proposed hepatitis B vaccine trial in Guinea-Bissau raises concerns about delaying newborn protection. This commentary examines the ethical obligations of researchers and the consequences of weakening established prevention efforts. For International Infection Prevention Week, Infection Control Today explores how prevention connects hospital departments with everyday community life and why infection preventionists (IPs), sterile processing department (SPD), professionals, and environmental services (EVS) teams deserve lasting support. This week in infection prevention: Kenya's imported Ebola case showed how fever screening can miss an ill traveler, Florida's dengue outbreak reached 296 local cases, and new guidance underscores that missed surfaces and shared equipment fuel AMR risk. Our weekly roundup covers these stories and more. During Sterile Processing Week, Infection Control Today honors the professionals behind safe instrument reprocessing and calls for year-round investment in education, staffing, resources, and meaningful collaboration across health care teams. In honor of Global Handwashing Day, Jamar Shaw, MD, MPH, CIC, explains how applying the WHO 5 Moments to actual care sequences can reduce transmission risks in ambulatory settings
